name: Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment
title: Portfolios, Performance Tasks, and Oral Assessment
answer: This idea is that tests alone cannot show everything students know and can do, so schools should also use portfolios, performance tasks, and oral assessments. Portfolios show growth over time, performance tasks ask students to apply knowledge to realistic problems, and oral assessments let students explain their understanding aloud. These methods matter because they give a fuller picture of learning while keeping teachers in charge of judging quality and fairness.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: The idea addresses the gap left when tests are the only measure of learning. Portfolios gather work across time, and students can add reflections that explain each piece, which helps show growth rather than a single score. Performance tasks ask students to use what they know in realistic situations, such as designing an experiment or building an argument from documents. Oral assessment asks students to explain their thinking, often by recording a short video about how they solved a problem. Together these approaches capture parts of knowing and doing that tests may miss, while AI can assist with summarizing or drafting rather than replacing teacher judgment.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, students can build digital portfolios in Google Sites and write reflections on each piece, and AI may help summarize patterns across a portfolio, but the student's own reflections are treated as the most meaningful part. For performance tasks, a science class might ask students to design an experiment, while a history class might ask them to build an argument from documents. Teachers can use MagicSchool to draft performance tasks and rubrics, then check that the task measures the intended skills and is fair to all students. For oral assessment, a student might record a short video explaining how they solved a problem, with recordings made on school devices and stored on school systems. The text does not give grade bands for these practices, so they are described generally.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not provide a study, figure, or formal evidence label for portfolios, performance tasks, or oral assessment. It presents these approaches as practice rather than as claims backed by research. The one finding it states is that automated scoring of speech can misjudge students with accents or developing language, as Chapter 13 described. That point is used to support teacher scoring of oral assessments, not to claim that the broader assessment methods have been proven by a study.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that AI should not take over the judgments that matter most. AI can summarize portfolio patterns, but the student's reflections carry the most meaning. AI can help draft performance tasks and rubrics, but the teacher must check that the task measures the intended skills and is fair to all students. Oral assessments must be scored by the teacher, because automated scoring of speech can misjudge students with accents or developing language. Recordings should be made on school devices and stored on school systems, and the decisions about what counts as evidence of learning stay with the teacher.
